title: TF deploy sanity probes and flaky dependency playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact playbook for quick sanity probes and hypothesis-driven troubleshooting during private (VPC / on-prem) Terraform-driven installs and upgrades. Focus: fast detection of flaky external deps (NTP, DNS, container registry), TF race conditions, and common runtime failures (driver/kernel mismatches, docker/containerd flakiness, networking MTU issues).

Scope / When to use:
- preflight before any customer-facing upgrade (apply or rolling update)
- first-responder checklist when an install hangs or post-upgrade capacity errors appear
- capture minimal reproducible evidence for SRE/infra handoff

Quick checklist (run in sequence, aim for 10-20 minutes):
1) Confirm control-plane reachability:
   - ssh to bootstrap host or bastion (check ~/.ssh and agent forwarded keys)
   - curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health or service health endpoints behind local proxy
2) Terraform sanity: plan -> refresh -> apply dry-run
   - terraform init -backend-config=... && terraform workspace show
   - terraform validate && terraform plan -out=tf.plan || capture plan.err
   - terraform apply -auto-approve tf.plan only after plan sanity
3) Registry and artifact pulls:
   - docker pull/ctr pull the container images used in module (ensure registry auth is working)
   - check token expiry: cat /etc/docker/config.json or credential helper logs
4) DNS, NTP, and proxy checks:
   - dig +short registry.company.internal; if empty, verify /etc/resolv.conf and systemd-resolved status
   - chronyc tracking || timedatectl status (avoid skew > 5s for cert/TLS issues)
5) Kernel & GPU drivers (if applicable):
   - nvidia-smi || dmesg | grep -i nvrm
   - modinfo nvidia || lsmod | grep nvidia
   - uname -r vs. kernel-headers for dkms builds
6) CNI / MTU checks:
   - ip link show && ip -s link show <iface> (look for fragmentation if MTU mismatch)
   - curl --max-time 5 http://10.0.0.1:port to test pod-to-pod networking across hosts
7) Container runtime health:
   - systemctl status containerd/docker
   - journalctl -u containerd --since "10m" | tail -n 200
8) Minimal functional smoke (end-to-end):
   - curl POST to inference /generate endpoint with a 10-token prompt over the same network path customers will use
   - assert HTTP 200 and response length > 8 tokens; record latency

Terraform module caveats & red flags (common root causes):
- provider plugin race: mixing 'local-exec' that depends on ephemeral resources often races with resource creation. If apply fails intermittently, set explicit depends_on or split into two plans.
- state drift after failed apply: partial resources can cause future applies to hit duplicates. Use terraform state list and import/taint rather than manual deletion unless guided.
- module version skew across teams: older modules reference deprecated auth methods (e.g., legacy token headers). Confirm module versions pinned in root module.
- provider auth refresh failures: long-running plans hitting expired STS tokens. Short-term mitigation: increase credential lifetime or run 'aws sts get-caller-identity' from the host to confirm.

Failure fingerprints and immediate next steps:
- Symptom: terraform apply hangs at 'creating module...':
  - quick probe: check API rate-limits (cloudprovider dashboards), run 'terraform apply -target=module.x -refresh=true' to isolate
  - likely: cloud provider throttling / missing quotas
  - mitigation: retry with throttling backoff, escalate to cloud account owner for quota bump

- Symptom: pods stuck in CrashLoopBackOff after upgrade:
  - check container logs (kubectl -n redwood logs pod -p)
  - check image digest mismatch vs tag (digest immutability), registry auth failure shows quay/docker login errors
  - mitigation: if image pull secrets invalid, reapply k8s secret with updated credentials, drain and force-recreate pods

- Symptom: intermittent TLS handshake failures between services:
  - check clock skew and certificate expiry; verify MTU/path MTU causes truncation of TLS handshake
  - tcpdump on host (tcpdump -nni any port 443) and compare packet sizes
  - mitigation: fix NTP, or set MSS clamping in CNI/edge routers temporarily

- Symptom: GPUs visible but runtime errors in model load:
  - look for mismatched CUDA, cuDNN, and python wheel versions in container logs
  - dmesg for OOM/killer or firmware messages; sometimes driver updates required after kernel upgrades
  - mitigation: pin runtime images to validated combinations; if urgent, failover to CPU-only node pool

Evidence capture (must include these in the initial ticket):
- terraform plan output and exact command used (paste tf plan -out and plan.log)
- controller/agent logs (last 1k lines each), container runtime journal output
- kernel dmesg and /var/log/messages/syslog (timestamps around failure)
- output of the 8 quick probes above (stdout + return codes)

Minimal probe scripts (copy locally and run):
- quick-health.sh (example):
  #!/bin/bash
  set -euo pipefail
  echo "health:"; curl -sS -w '\\nHTTP_CODE:%{http_code}\\nTIME_MS:%{time_total}' -X POST http://localhost:8080/generate -d '{"prompt":"ping"}' || true
  echo "docker version:"; docker version || ctr version || true
  echo "nvidia-smi:"; nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,driver_version --format=csv,noheader || true

- tf-plan-diff.sh (example):
  #!/bin/bash
  terraform plan -input=false -no-color -out=tf.plan && terraform show -json tf.plan | jq -r '.resource_changes[]?.type + " " + (.address // "")' || true

Rolling upgrade quick rollback pattern:
- Never delete state; do a _controlled_ rollback by applying the previous module version with explicit apply -target where necessary.
- If rolling k8s workload upgrade fails, use kubectl rollout undo and revert image tag immediately; do not delete ReplicaSets until healthy rollback is confirmed.

Escalation matrix (fast path):
- 0-30 mins: on-call eng-private-deployments (pager) + author of last tf change
- 30-90 mins: SRE + infra-eng for cloud quota / routing / peering issues
- >90 mins: Incident lead and account manager for customer communication, escalate to platform eng for code-level fixes

Runbook additions to submit after each incident:
- exact terraform commands + git sha used for modules
- one-line hypothesis that matched observed symptoms
- a blameless summary and next three actions to prevent recurrence

Open questions / notes for future improvements:
- automated small-scale TF dry-run that validates registry auth without touching state (prototype suggested in PR 612)
- add a TTL-based probe that exercises GPU hot-path (warm model load) during upgrades to catch binary mismatches earlier
- centralize 'probe outputs' S3/artifact upload for faster postmortems

Last-minute reminders for on-call: keep the initial ticket short and attach raw logs; avoid early mass restarts — prefer targeted resource recreates and controlled reverts.

Document history: initial draft 2024-11-07 by Aisha Patel; input from Marcus and Diego added 2024-12; updated remediation patterns 2025-01-22.
